members.assessment: Wu is the grandfather loved by Minhuai and the predecessor of Hui. Source106 correctly keeps the pigpen emperor with Wu and distinguishes the later funeral speaker Hui from his cited 先帝/聖祖/皇祖.

After Xuan/Jing/Wen, Wu follows Han/Wei mourning precedent in the new Jin court; Sima Fu and the named founding ministers address him. This is the founding Jin ruler, not Cao Cao or another dynasty’s Wu.
Later Jin ritualists quote 武皇帝故事 and the Xianning edict, with Taishi10/Taikang7 examples. Later speakers and reigns do not change the earlier edict’s owner.
Huan Qian in An’s Yuanxing1 reign explicitly reviews 武皇帝詔 and contrasts it with post-restoration habits. Wu is the prior Western Jin edict-maker; AD402 dates the quoted later memorial, not Wu’s life.
Wu rules on Guo Yi’s posthumous name in Taikang8, after the explicit Jin dynastic discussion and before a later Taiyuan precedent. This is the same Jin Wu.
Jin succession and Taishi precede the closing sequence 終武、惠、孝懷三世. The first Jin ruler Wu in this explicit reign sequence is the predecessor of Hui/Huai, not an isolated generic 武.
The explicit 晉受命 武帝 reorganizes the library and appoints Miao Zheng; Xianning4 academy foundations belong to the same Wu before Hui’s Yongping/Yuankang changes.

武帝字安世 is an individual courtesy-name anchor. His empress inhabits the earlier Wei Anshi Hall; He Zeng’s criticism predicts the later Yongxi/Yongjia dynastic collapse. The founding Jin ruler is intended.
Early Wu with He Zeng/He Shao/Wang Kai and 武帝泰始七年 points to the same Western Jin court. Hui’s later Yuankang is a separate sequel.
Wu promotes Wang Jun as Dragon-Loft General and conquers Sun Hao’s Wu; the Taikang context and contrast with later Yuan identify Jin Wu, not Sun Wu as a personal identity.

The Hui Yongxi omen narrative links the two-fire gloss to 武帝’s taboo and 蘭 to the Yang empress in Yang Jun’s fall. It refers retrospectively to Hui’s Western Jin predecessor. No unsupported identification of which Yang empress is added to the identity proposal.
Explicit 武帝太康九年 and 武帝太康五年, plus the reproach for ignoring He Jiao and keeping Hui as heir, identify the same Jin Wu. An isolated 帝 is governed by that explicit Wu frame.
Zuo Fen’s palace and Yuan Empress Yang elegy dated Taishi10 identify the consort’s emperor as Jin Wu. 聖皇 and 帝 in the poem remain that husband; legendary model queens in nearby lines are comparisons.

The same empress elegy speaks of 帝與后, their earlier humble household and purple halls, and ends 元后. In the supplied Zuo Fen/Yuan Empress frame this emperor is Wu. No ancient exemplary ruler from other poetic comparisons is substituted.

The Xianning2 Dao-empress praise, Taishi9 palace selections, Hu Fen’s daughter, Wu conquest/Sun Hao palace women and Zhuge Wan investiture all concern the same Jin Wu. His royal daughter Wannian and consort-family relations are consistent; Wu speaks in s0506 while Fang answers in s0507.

武帝受禪 when Chenliu leaves the throne is the founding Jin ruler; subsequent emperor references honor Sima Fu through Taishi8 and enfeoff Sima Wang. Fu’s declaration as Wei’s loyal minister is his own speech, not a different Wu.
The ruler at 武帝受禪 enfeoffs Hong/Mao, with Zheng’s later posthumous Sui enfeoffment in the same Jin princely sequence. Zheng, not Wu, is the recipient of the s0195 title.

These princes pass from Wei office to Wu’s abdication/accession enfeoffments and Taishi2 domains. The statement that Yi died before Wu’s accession dates Yi, not Wu, and does not introduce another emperor.

Repeated 武帝受禪 enfeoffs Gui/Gui/Heng/Jing/Quan; Taishi era and Sima Fu household frame identify one Jin emperor across the duplicated records. The mourned prince in s0278 is Gui; the mourning 帝 remains Wu.
Tai moves from Wei office to 武帝受禪 Longxi enfeoffment, later Taikang and Yongxi. Wu is the founding Jin enfeoffer, not Tai or the later crown prince.
Sui serves Wei, then 武帝受禪 makes him Prince of Jinan before his Taishi2 death. This is the founding Jin Wu.
Xun serves Wei, receives Wu’s accession enfeoffment as Prince of Qiao, and dies Taishi2. The same founding Jin Wu is the enfeoffer.
Mu serves Wei then 武帝受禪 enfeoffs Zhongshan; the ensuing temple debate is governed by that Jin accession court and distinguishes named ancestors from the reigning emperor.
武帝踐阼，泰始中 and Sun He’s recommendation of Can explicitly place this ruler at the Jin accession/Taishi court.
Wu appoints Guo Qi; Qi later refuses Zhao Lun because 我已為武帝吏. The explicit retrospect and different usurper distinguish the same former Jin emperor from Lun.
武帝太康六年 is used retrospectively to date Murong Gui’s ducal title within a later Murong Wei account. The Wu/Taikang ruler is Jin Wu; neither Gui nor Wei is that emperor.

The Tang memorial defending Chu Suiliang explicitly cites 晉武 and Liu Yi as an older toleration precedent, parallel with 漢祖/周昌. Jin Wu is the historical comparator; the Tang addressee 陛下 is a distinct person.
